CPN-HRL :a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning approach for priority–aware task scheduling in CPN enabled by cloud–edge–end environments
Qiqiang Yue1 · Le Tian1,2,3,4 · Xu Feng1 · Zheng Yuan1,2,3,4 · Shuai Wei1 · Jiqiang Xia1 · Bo Chen1,2,3,4 · Xuanyan Song1,2,3,4 · Ying Yao1 · Yi Liu5
Received: 20 January 2026 / Accepted: 19 March 2026 © The Author(s) 2026
Abstract A Computing Power Network (CPN) is a cloud–edge–end integrated infrastructure that interconnects heterogeneous com- puting resources to support latency-sensitive and volatile workloads. A core challenge in CPN task scheduling is to jointly determine task prioritization and computational node selection under dynamic arrivals, resource heterogeneity, and multi- objective conflicts. In this paper, we study dynamic task scheduling in a CPN and aim to (i) minimize average task completion time, (ii) maximize scheduling success rate under deadline constraints, and (iii) improve global resource utilization. We propose CPN-HRL, a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework that decomposes scheduling into two coordinated subproblems: a high-level agent (LSTM-PPO) generates global priority weights for queued tasks, and a low-level agent (GAT-PPO) performs topology-aware node selection for each task in the ranked sequence. To further guarantee timeliness for latency-critical tasks, we introduce a two-queue mechanism with an Urgent Queue and a Main Queue, together with a dynamic reordering trigger. Simulation results on multiple real-world topologies show that, under our experimental settings, CPN-HRL reduces average completion time and maintains high scheduling success rate under high loads, while improving overall resource utilization.
Keywords Computing power networks · Priority-aware scheduling · Hierarchical deep reinforcement learning · Resource allocation
1 Introduction
With the advancement of technologies such as the Industrial Internet, Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence, emerg- ing application scenarios have seen an explosive growth in demand for computing power, making it increasingly dif- ficult for single computing facilities to meet these needs. Computing power networks (Yukun et al. 2024; Tang et al. 2021; Huijuan et al. 2021; Bo et al. 2019), as a new type of information infrastructure integrating multi-dimensional heterogeneous computing resources across cloud, edge, and endpoint, have become pivotal to supporting the digital econ- omy. However, computing network environments exhibit high dynamism and complexity, presenting the following chal- lenges for task scheduling:
1. Task Heterogeneity and Dynamic Priority Adapta- tion: Tasks vary significantly in resource requirements, urgency, data volume, and latency sensitivity, necessitat- ing dynamic determination of scheduling priorities (Feng et al. 2024); 2. Resource Heterogeneity: Computing nodes exhibit un- even distribution in processing capabilities, geographic locations, and load states (He et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2022); 3. Multi-Objective Constraints: Simultaneous optimiza- tion of multiple often-conflicting objectives such as average task completion time, task success rate, and resource utilization is required (Wang et al. 2025); 4. Dynamic Uncertainty: Random task arrivals and con- tinuously changing resource states demand scheduling algorithms (Koslovski et al. 2024; Mande et al. 2024) with online decision-making and adaptive capabilities.
The task scheduling problem in computing grids fun- damentally belongs to complex combinatorial optimization problems, requiring the identification of optimal solutions that satisfy constraints within finite resource allocation schemes. This constitutes an NP-hard problem. Traditional mathematical approaches such as integer programming and dynamic programming struggle to efficiently compute exact solutions. Meanwhile, classical heuristic rules like First- Come-First-Served (FCFS) fail to adapt to dynamic envi- ronments. Although metaheuristic algorithms like Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) (Alsaidy et al. 2022; Zhan and Huo 2012) and Genetic Algorithms (GA) (Behera and Sob- hanayak 2024; Pang et al. 2019) can handle multi-objective optimization, they suffer from slow convergence rates and complex parameter tuning, making them unsuitable for real- time scheduling demands.
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns optimal poli- cies through interaction with the environment. Leveraging its robust environmental perception and decision-making capabilities,ithasbeenappliedtoschedulingproblems,prov- ing particularly effective for intelligent decision-making in dynamic environments. However, single-layer DRL models (Sheng et al. 2021) such as DQN and DDPG often suffer fromthecurseofdimensionalityandtraininginstabilitywhen dealing with large action spaces. Moreover, these models struggle to effectively balance the two critical factors of pri- ority assignment and node selection simultaneously.
The methods for task priority sorting can be categorized into two types: pre-scheduling sorting (Xie et al. 2025) and local scheduling sorting (Feng et al. 2024). The former is performed by the network control center based on global
state information prior to task execution, during which prior- ity allocation or classification is conducted within the global buffer queue. Computing nodes then execute tasks sequen- tially, without requiring complex queuing or reordering mechanisms. In contrast, the latter approach performs final sorting at the computing node after task assignment, accord- ing to a local queuing strategy. However, due to the absence of global coordination, this method is prone to load imbal- ance. Additionally, queuing tasks upon arrival at the node introduces extra end-to-end latency, which is particularly detrimental to delay-sensitive tasks and ultimately reduces overall scheduling efficiency. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a pre-scheduling sorting mechanism that responds to the critical requirements of delay-sensitive appli- cations by leveraging global information to achieve efficient and low-latency task scheduling.
To address the aforementioned issues, we propose a hier- archical deep reinforcement learning scheduling algorithm.
1. We propose a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that decouples global task prioritization from local resource allocation. This design enables an effi- cient task scheduling algorithm capable of adapting to the dynamic environment of computational networks, sig- nificantly reducing decision complexity while achieving efficient task execution and optimal resource utilization. 2. We treat task prioritization and node selection as high- levelandlow-leveltaskswithinahierarchicalframework, modeling them respectively as MDPs to learn joint poli- cies. The high-level agent employs an LSTM as its policy network to consider long-term benefits and learn priority weights from a global perspective; The lower-level agent employs GAT for feature embedding, focusing on imme- diate benefits to achieve precise resource allocation for each ranked task. Both upper and lower-level agents uti- lize the PPO reinforcement learning algorithm for policy optimization. 3. We designed a multi-level queue management mecha- nism integrating emergency queues with the main queue, along with a dynamic reordering trigger mechanism, to ensure the scheduling requirements of high-urgency tasks. 4. Simulation experiments validate that the CPN-HRL algo- rithm outperforms multiple baseline algorithms across several core performance metrics.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews relevant research on task scheduling, including rule- based and learning-based approaches; Section 3 introduces the system model and presents the problem model; Section 4 elaborates on the algorithm design; Section 5 analyzes and discusses simulation results; Section 6 summarizes the paper and outlines future work.

2 Related works and motivation
Task scheduling is a critical challenge in computing power networks, with related research based on two approaches: rule-based and learning-based methods.
2.1 Rule-based approach
Early research on task scheduling in computing networks primarily relied on heuristic rules, meta-heuristic algo- rithms, and game theory approaches. Heuristic rules such as FCFS and HEFT (Gupta et al. 2022) gained widespread adoption due to their low computational overhead and sim- plicity of implementation. However, they lack systematic globalstateawareness,resultinginlimitedschedulingperfor- mance within highly heterogeneous and dynamic computing network environments where tasks and resources exhibit sig- nificant heterogeneity.
To enhance scheduling quality, meta-heuristic algorithms were introduced to intelligently search the solution space for optimal scheduling schemes. For instance, Ref. Wu et al. (2019) proposed a cloud-edge collaborative computing offloading model based on improved particle swarm opti- mization for mobile edge computing scenarios, dynamically adjusting inertial weights to balance task latency and energy costs; Ref. Mousavi et al. (2022) proposed an improved NSGA-II algorithm incorporating a recombination opera- tor to optimize dual objectives: server energy consumption and overall response time. However, meta-heuristic algo- rithms exhibit performance sensitivity to parameter tuning and suffer from slow convergence, making them ill-suited for low-latencyrequirementsinlarge-scalereal-timescheduling. Additionally, game theory has been applied to distributed scheduling scenarios. Ref. Yang et al. (2020) based on game theory,ataskschedulingalgorithmthatbalancestaskreliabil- ity is proposed. A computational node task scheduling model is constructed, applying game strategies to computational node rate allocation within a cooperative game framework.
In summary, traditional rule-based methods prove sim- ple and effective in specific static scenarios. However, when confronting the high dynamism, heterogeneity, and multi- objective conflicts inherent in computing networks, they exhibit significant limitations in adaptability, convergence speed, and real-time performance. Furthermore, they fail to account for the priority attributes of composite tasks.
2.2 Learning-based approach
With the advancement of artificial intelligence technol- ogy, learning-based methods represented by deep reinforce- ment learning (DRL) offer novel solutions for dynamic task scheduling through robust environmental perception and decision-making capabilities. In existing research, Ref.
Cheng et al. (2022) applies DRL to hybrid cloud real-time job scheduling, jointly optimizing cost, response time, and service success rate; Ref. Zou et al. (2022) constructs a computation-priority network architecture, modeling multi- user scheduling on heterogeneous computing resources as a multi-objective Markov decision process solved via DRL; Ref. Xie et al. (2025) proposes a priority-aware scheduling scheme based on enhanced DRL for edge computing sys- tems in computing networks to improve task success rates and resource utilization.
A recent body of work in intelligent IoE and 6G edge environments has shifted towards AI-native coordination for task allocation and device selection under heterogeneous and dynamic conditions. For instance, Ref (Jamil et al. 2025) proposes an intelligent resource selection strategy that explicitlyanalyzesdeviceselectiondelay,computationaleffi- ciency, and task success rates as key performance indicators in dense edge networks. These frameworks often leverage learning-based components to adapt to highly volatile traffic and resource availability at the network edge.However, such IoE/edge-oriented approaches primarily address localized scheduling within a limited set of interconnected nodes, and typically do not incorporate multi-domain topology aware- ness or hierarchical decision-making for global prioritization across diverse queue types.
Moreover, these studies predominantly employ single- layer DRL architectures that couple decision-making tasks such as priority ranking and node selection, which leads to an exponential increase in the action space as task and node scales grow, resulting in the curse of dimensionality and policy convergence difficulties and thus limiting their applicability in large-scale computing networks.
Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) achieves decou- pling by decomposing complex decisions into high- and low-level subtasks. High-level agents make infrequent deci- sions to optimize long-term returns, while low-level agents execute high-frequency actions to achieve short-term goals. Its effectiveness has been validated in resource allocation scenarios such as virtual network embedding (Wang et al. 2023, 2024). Inspired by this approach, we addresses the urgency requirements of latency-sensitive tasks by adopting a pre- scheduling sorting mechanism. Leveraging global informa- tion, it achieves efficient, low-latency task scheduling. we proposes introducing a hierarchical architecture into com- puting power network task scheduling. It establishes a col- laborative model where high-level agents handle macro-level priority sorting of responsible tasks, while low-level agents focus on real-time, fine-grained node selection. A hierarchi- cal deep reinforcement learning dynamic priority scheduling algorithm is designed to enhance the scheduling efficiency and performance of large-scale computing-network systems (Table 1).

C4 enforces deadline compliance by requiring each task’s completion time to satisfy its maximum tolerable delay, thereby linking scheduling decisions to the reliability
objective. C5 guarantees transmission feasibility by ensuring that the available bandwidth along the selected routing path meets task requirements, avoiding congestion-induced QoS violations.
Together, these constraints ensure that task prioritization and node selection decisions remain physically realizable, QoS-compliant, and consistent with network resource limi- tations.
4 DRL implement
To address the optimization problem proposed in Section 3, this section introduces a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm based on task priority.
The algorithm decouples global scheduling from local resource matching within a hierarchical reinforcement learn- ing framework (Fig. 4), constructing a two-layer MDP model: while the lower-layer GAT-PPO agent aggregates node topology and resource features using graph attention mechanisms to perform task-node matching under upper- layer constraints.
An interaction mechanism achieves global-local objec- tive alignment, while PPO pruning and GAE advantage estimation ensure training stability, ultimately enabling col- laborative optimization of multiple scheduling objectives. Subsequent sections detail the design principles and train- ing methods for both upper- and lower-layer agents.

5.2.3 Scalability analysis
To validate the applicability of CPN-HRL across networks of varying scales, we conducted tests under four distinct topologies: Abilene, GEANT, Switch, and ChinaNet. The HEFT algorithm showed significant improvement over FCFS but still under- performed other DRL algorithms in dynamic environments. Regarding scheduling success rate, CPN-HRL maintained a rate of 80% – 90% even as network scale increased, demon- strating a clear advantage over other algorithms.

under complex network topologies. The hierarchical archi- tecture of CPN-HRL effectively mitigates the curse of dimensionality, offering excellent scalability to meet the demands of large-scale computing networks.

6 Summary and future work
6.1 Technical contributions
In this paper, we proposed CPN-HRL, a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework for priority-aware task scheduling in computing power networks (CPN). The key contribution lies in decomposing a coupled combinatorial scheduling problem into two coordinated subproblems: (i) global dynamic task prioritization and (ii) topology-aware computing node selection. This hierarchical decomposition mitigates the curse of dimensionality encountered in con- ventional reinforcement learning approaches, while enabling structured coordination between long-term global objec- tives (e.g., success rate and load balance) and short-term local decisions (node-level feasibility and delay minimiza- tion).TheintegrationofLSTM-basedtemporalmodelingand GAT-based topology embedding further enhances the repre- sentation capacity of the scheduling agents under dynamic and heterogeneous environments.
Simulation results across multiple network topologies indicate that the proposed framework improves scheduling efficiency and maintains stable performance under varying load conditions within the evaluated scenarios.
6.2 Security boundary and deployment assumptions
While the proposed framework focuses on QoS-aware scheduling optimization, practical deployment of centralized CPNcontrolmechanismsnecessitatesexplicitclarificationof security scope and operational assumptions.
6.2.1 Threat model
We consider three categories of potential threats in CPN envi- ronments:
(1) Task manipulation attacks,where malicious users sub-
mit falsified task attributes (e.g., deadlines, bandwidth requirements, or priority flags) to gain unfair scheduling advantages or overload specific nodes; (2) Telemetry manipulation attacks:where node resource
states or link measurements are spoofed or partially cor- rupted, leading to incorrect state observations for the reinforcement learning agents; (3) Controller-centric attacks,including denial-of-service
(DoS)targetingthecentralizedcontrolcenterorattempts to extract model parameters of the trained policies.
6.2.2 Security assumptions
Inthiswork,weassumeauthenticatedtasksourcesandsecure communication channels between routing nodes and the cen-
tralized controller. Under these assumptions, we focus on scheduling policy optimization rather than end-to-end net- work security protocol design.
6.2.3 Security scope of DL-based scheduling
The high-level (LSTM-PPO) and low-level (GAT-PPO) agents operate on observed system states. Their robust- ness depends on the reliability of telemetry inputs and task descriptors. Therefore, the DL models themselves are not designed as intrusion detection mechanisms but as decision- making modules within a trusted control framework.
Recent AI-based network threat detection frameworks (Paracha et al. 2024) demonstrate that machine learning mod- els can analyze traffic patterns and behavioral anomalies to proactively identify cyber attacks and support forensic investigation and mitigation strategies. Inspired by these approaches, a practical CPN deployment can integrate an AI- driven anomaly detection module as a front-end filter before the scheduling pipeline to detect abnormal task submissions or telemetryinconsistencies. Suchintegrationwouldenhance system resilience without altering the hierarchical scheduling design proposed in this paper.
6.3 Future work
Future research can extend this work in several directions:
(1) Security-awarescheduling:Integratinganomalydetec-
tion outputs into the HRL state space and designing robust policies against adversarial perturbations; (2) Reliability-constrained optimization: Incorporating
risk-sensitive objectives (e.g., CVaR) to satisfy ultra- reliable low-latency service requirements; (3) Decentralized or federated control architectures:
Reducing centralized attack surfaces while maintaining global coordination. (4) Real-world deployment validation: Evaluating sche-
duling overhead, telemetry delay, and imperfect moni- toring in operational CPN environments.

To test the algorithm’s robustness under varying system loads, we conducted experiments on the ChinaNet topology. The task arrival rate λ was gradually increased from 5 tasks per time slot to 15 tasks per time slot. We observed changes in three core metrics, with detailed results shown in Fig. 6.

To validate the applicability of CPN-HRL across networks of varying scales, we conducted tests under four distinct topologies: Abilene, GEANT, Switch, and ChinaNet. We maintained a fixed task arrival rate of λ = 10 to ensure testing under moderate system load conditions. As shown in Fig. 7(a), (b), and (c), the performance of all algo- rithms deteriorates as the network scale increases. However, CPN-HRL exhibits the smallest decline and consistently maintains robust performance. Regarding average task com- pletion time, CPN-HRL achieved the shortest average task completion time across all four network topologies, outper- forming the PSO-DQN algorithm by 9.8% – 12.3% and the PATD3 algorithm by 11.7% – 13.6%. The HEFT algorithm showed significant improvement over FCFS but still under- performed other DRL algorithms in dynamic environments. Regarding scheduling success rate, CPN-HRL maintained a rate of 80% – 90% even as network scale increased, demon- strating a clear advantage over other algorithms.

We specifically evaluated the algorithm’s scheduling perfor- mance for urgent tasks. Under the GEANT topology, with a fixed task arrival rate of λ = 10 and we have increased the proportion of emergency tasks from 0.1 to 0.5, as shown in Fig. 8 , CPN-HRL leverages its multi-level queueing mech- anism and reordering trigger mechanism to provide priority response for urgent tasks.Its regular task success rate reached 91.2% Its urgent task success rate reached 70.5%, with an average response time of only 18.5ms. In contrast, static priority-based algorithms like HEFT, as well as single-layer reinforcement learning algorithms such as SAC and PATD3, failed to guarantee timely scheduling for urgent tasks, result- ing in task failures.
